claims.quote: Japan Air Lines Cargo Flight 1628 was a Japanese Boeing 747-200 cargo aircraft flying from Paris Charles De Gaulle Airport to Narita International Airport that was involved in an unidentified flying object (UFO) sighting on 17 November 1986.

Japan Air Lines Cargo Flight 1628 was a Japanese Boeing 747-200 cargo aircraft flying from Paris Charles De Gaulle Airport to Narita International Airport that was involved in an unidentified flying object (UFO) sighting on 17 November 1986.

On the Reykjavík to Anchorage section of the flight at 17:11 over eastern Alaska, pilot Kenji Terauchi reported seeing three unidentified objects flying at 35,000 feet (11,000 m), which were "flying parallel and then ... very close".

claims.v: Reykjavík to Anchorage
claims.quote: On the Reykjavík to Anchorage section of the flight at 17:11 over eastern Alaska, pilot Kenji Terauchi reported seeing three unidentified objects flying at 35,000 feet (11,000 m), which were "flying parallel and then ... very close".

claims.v: six minutes
claims.quote: After six minutes, Terauchi radioed the Anchorage Federal Aviation Administration who advised him to take "evasive action" after seeing the objects on their radar.

claims.v: 640 kilometres (400 miles)
claims.quote: Terauchi reported that the objects followed the plane for 640 kilometres (400 miles) and described what he perceived as rapid movements and sudden stops.

claims.v: advised the pilot to take "evasive action"
claims.quote: After six minutes, Terauchi radioed the Anchorage Federal Aviation Administration who advised him to take "evasive action" after seeing the objects on their radar.

claims.v: decreased altitude and circled the cargo plane; lights reportedly remained with the aircraft
claims.quote: Terauchi decreased altitude and circled his cargo plane, but reported that the lights were still with his aircraft even after the manoeuvres.

claims.v: news media stated that the FAA reported seeing objects near the plane even after the evasive manoeuvres
claims.quote: At the time, news media stated that the FAA reported seeing objects near the plane even after the evasive manoeuvres, but upon later review, the military radar images were "dismissed as clutter, and an object that showed up on the aviation agency's screens was thought to be a coincidental split image of the aircraft".

Both the FAA and Air Force confirmed that the unidentified flying objects appeared on their radars.

On the Reykjavík to Anchorage section of the flight at 17:11 over eastern Alaska, pilot Kenji Terauchi reported seeing three unidentified objects flying at 35,000 feet (11,000 m), which were "flying parallel and then ... very close".
Klass noted that the crew were interviewed separately in 1988 and asserts their remembrance of the event differed significantly.
Terauchi reported that the objects followed the plane for 640 kilometres (400 miles) and described what he perceived as rapid movements and sudden stops.
Flight 1628 landed in Anchorage, the crew were debriefed, and FAA investigators determined that they were "normal, professional, rational, (and had) no drug or alcohol involvement".
Some astronomers and investigators believe that Terauchi probably mistook the planets Jupiter and Mars as UFOs.

claims.v: Jupiter was only 10 degrees above the horizon
claims.quote: Klass states that it is not unusual for an experienced pilot to "[mistake] a bright celestial body for a UFO, nor will it be the last. ... Jupiter was only 10 degrees above the horizon, making it appear to the pilot to be roughly at his own 35,000-foot altitude".

claims.v: Jupiter and Mars
claims.quote: Editor of Aviation Week and Space Technology magazine and UFO investigator Phillip J. Klass reported that the planets Jupiter and Mars were in the area that Terauchi said he saw two lights, and although they would have been quite visible, he did not mention seeing them.

At the time, news media stated that the FAA reported seeing objects near the plane even after the evasive manoeuvres, but upon later review, the military radar images were "dismissed as clutter, and an object that showed up on the aviation agency's screens was thought to be a coincidental split image of the aircraft".
